decision.chose: 12 phases with separate INTAKE, CLARIFY, PLAN, PARALLELIZE, BASELINE, EXECUTE, RESOLVE, VERIFY, REVIEW, FIX, RECAPTURE, DELIVER.
decision.rejected: 9-phase variant collapsing CLARIFY into PLAN (planner improvises questions inline) and merging RECAPTURE into DELIVER (one combined "ship it" step).
decision.rationale: CLARIFY needs an `AskUserQuestion` boundary the planner cannot cross alone — folding it into PLAN blocks parallel waves because each planner stops to wait for human input. Splitting BASELINE / RECAPTURE from EXECUTE / DELIVER keeps the visual-evidence pair atomic across the fix loop: the same outline color and viewport shape are reused for the after-screenshot, which a single combined phase would obscure. Twelve phases let each prompt file own one verb and one verdict.

decision.chose: Every phase fronts exactly one versioned prompt file under `prompts/NN-<phase>.md`; the orchestrator dispatches by `Agent({prompt: read(prompts/05-task-executor.md) + parameter block})`.
decision.rejected: Inline orchestrator-typed prompts ("just write the prompt in the spawn call"); per-batch ad-hoc prompts living only in the run log; one mega-prompt covering all 12 phases switched by a `phase=` parameter.
decision.rationale: Multi-feature batches drift when the orchestrator improvises long prompts each time — instructions evolve, drift becomes invisible, and parallelism collapses to "one feature at a time, manually narrated." Versioned files give each phase a deterministic capability the orchestrator composes. They also pin behaviour to a SHA so post-mortems can reproduce a run, and they keep prompt diffs reviewable in code review instead of buried in chat history. A single mega-prompt loses both per-phase verdicts (`done=`, `verdict=`) and the ability to swap one phase's prompt without touching others.

decision.chose: Every parallel executor runs in its own `git worktree add <isolated path> -b feature/<id> <default-branch>` and removes the worktree after merging.
decision.rejected: Single shared working tree with serialized executors (no parallelism gain); per-executor full clones (3-5x disk cost, no shared `.git/`); branch-only isolation in the main tree (concurrent agents corrupt each other's index and dev-toggle files).
decision.rationale: The main working tree carries uncommitted local-only state — preview data, `scheduled_tasks.lock`, dev toggles, the user's WIP. Concurrent agents touching it would corrupt each other and lose the user's work. Worktrees give each agent a clean, branch-scoped checkout sharing the same `.git/` for cheap branching. They also let the orchestrator run validators inside the worktree before merging — a failed verify aborts at the worktree boundary without ever touching main.

decision.chose: Wave merges into the default branch are serialized with `flock /tmp/faion-network-merge.lock` wrapping `fetch + rebase + ff-only merge`.
decision.rejected: Optimistic concurrent merges with retry on push failure (race conditions corrupt the index, especially mid-rebase); a dedicated merge-coordinator subagent (extra hop without solving the index-corruption root cause); push-only-from-worktrees (loses the local-merge invariant, requires remote round-trip per merge).
decision.rationale: Two simultaneous `git checkout main + merge` calls in the same `.git/` corrupt the index even when the merges themselves are conflict-free. `flock` is the cheapest correctness primitive: it serializes the index-mutating section only, not the long-running compute (validators, tests, builds) inside the worktree. The lock file is named per-repo (`/tmp/faion-network-merge.lock`) so different repositories merge in parallel.

decision.chose: VERIFY → REVIEW → FIX iterates with a hard cap (default 3); on cap-hit the feature is parked back in `todo/` with a written escalation note rather than looping further.
decision.rejected: Unbounded loop until PASS (burns quota and produces "polishing" diffs that obscure the original intent); single-pass review with no fix loop (drops every nit and forces the human reviewer to babysit); auto-merge on FAIL-WITH-NITS (silently lowers the quality bar).
decision.rationale: A quality gate without a hard cap becomes an infinite-cost search. Three iterations cover the common cases (typo, missing test, lint nit) without letting a wedged feature consume the whole batch's quota budget. The escalation back to `todo/` preserves the SDD artifacts intact so the next session resumes from a known good baseline instead of a half-fixed branch.

decision.chose: BASELINE captures a focused before-screenshot with red CSS outline; RECAPTURE captures a matching after-screenshot with green outline; the pair is delivered out-of-band (`tg-send --photo` or PR description) with an explanatory caption.
decision.rejected: PR description text only ("changed button color from blue to green") — readers cannot scan; full-page screenshots without focus outline (the eye cannot find the changed region in a 4000px image); recording a video walkthrough (heavy, hard to embed in async review).
decision.rationale: Visual changes on a faion-network-hosted surface need evidence the human reviewer can scan in seconds. A focused outlined screenshot makes the diff legible without scrolling. The same viewport, selector, and outline-injection script run in BASELINE and RECAPTURE so the pair is directly comparable. For non-visual phases (knowledge methodology batch, backend ETL fix) the playbook declares both phases as skip — the orchestrator records the skip and continues.

decision.chose: Each delivery surface (faion-net-fe, faion-network knowledge, storybook, mediamanager-fe, ETL) ships a `playbooks/<surface>.md` declaring skipped phases, surface-specific verifiers, and surface-specific delivery channels — the workflow's phase order is invariant.
decision.rejected: One-size-fits-all workflow (BASELINE / RECAPTURE forced even for knowledge XML batches that have no visual surface — wastes a subagent and produces empty artifacts); per-surface forks of the entire workflow (drift across forks, every fix has to be applied in five places); inlining surface logic into the orchestrator (orchestrator size explodes, behaviour becomes opaque).
decision.rationale: The phase order encodes the universal SDD shape (intake → plan → execute → verify → deliver). Surface-specific behaviour is variation in *which* validator runs, *which* channel ships the artifact, and *which* phases are inert — not variation in the order. Playbooks adapt; they never restructure (anti-pattern §14.1). This keeps the orchestrator's routing logic small while letting new surfaces onboard with one new file.

decision.chose: Convergence re-derivation is a single append-only step INSIDE the bounded verify-review-fix loop, running once after the first PASS. It reads intent, assesses present code state, and may only write new `TASK_*.md`.
decision.rejected: A thirteenth phase after DELIVER (breaks the locked 12-phase decision of 2026-05-02 and moves the check past the point where the batch is already declared done); an LLM-judge verdict on spec-vs-implementation completeness (a non-deterministic gate that blocks delivery on a score, which is precisely the failure mode that killed the spec-as-source products); a pre-EXECUTE run (there is no present state to assess yet, so every unbuilt item reports as missing).
decision.rationale: The loop previously terminated at PASS, and PASS is a statement about the diff that was produced, not about the intent that was declared. Work silently dropped between PLAN and EXECUTE — a task never written, a requirement no task covered — is invisible to a reviewer reading a diff, because the missing thing left no trace in it. Re-deriving from intent against present state is the only pass that can see it. Confining the step to appending tasks keeps intent immutable, keeps the output reviewable as one kind of diff, and keeps the phase count where the earlier decision put it.

decision.chose: Subagent prompts default to a freeform report body with one machine-parsed last-line marker, with the format instruction placed in the prompt file's trailing `Output` section. Whole-message JSON is reserved for mechanical, list-shaped phases. Every parsed marker is regex- or enum-validated by the orchestrator before it is acted on.
decision.rejected: Three co-equal output options with "pick exactly one" (the previous skeleton wording — it let the most reasoning-heavy phases pick whole-message JSON); schema-constrained output everywhere for uniform parsing; trusting a well-formed marker without validating its content.
decision.rationale: A format instruction read before the work compresses the channel the work happens in, and the phases that lose most are the judgement-heavy ones — REVIEW, PLAN, merge resolution — which are also the ones a uniform-JSON policy would capture first. A tail-placed contract costs nothing and constrains nothing upstream of itself. The validation half is separate and equally load-bearing: shape guarantees say nothing about value, so a syntactically perfect `done=` line can still name a feature that was never dispatched or a commit that does not exist. Checking is one regex; not checking loses work silently and surfaces it phases later.

decision.chose: A third role — the coordinator — running as an independent subagent at every wave boundary inside EXECUTE, gating the next wave's dispatch with CLEAR / HOLD / ABORT. The phase list stays at twelve; prompt-file numbering continues past twelve because prompt files are capabilities, not phases.
decision.rejected: A thirteenth phase (already rejected on 2026-08-04, and a phase after DELIVER checks the merge point after every wave has landed on it); folding the checks into the orchestrator (it decided the wave grouping being checked and holds the executors' reports — that is not a check); extending the REVIEW phase to cover the boundary (REVIEW reads a feature's diff against its spec, which is a different question from whether the combination is sound); running the coordinator only when a batch has ≥2 waves (a single wave still merges into a tree the orchestrator has not re-read).
decision.rationale: Two gaps sit at the wave seam and neither is visible to the role that produces them. Executors verify inside isolated worktrees, so each feature is proven green alone while the combination is unproven until VERIFY — which runs once, after every wave has already landed, with the merges stacked over any break and attribution gone. And wave admission is computed against the pre-batch tree, so a grouping that was disjoint when computed can be overlapping by the time it dispatches, surfacing as a conflict or a silent overwrite rather than as a scheduling decision. Both are cheap to catch at the boundary — one read of the merged tree — and expensive to catch anywhere else. Modelling it as a role rather than a phase is what keeps the check before every subsequent merge instead of after all of them, and preserves the 2026-05-02 phase-count decision intact. The coordinator is confined to reads plus two append-only files for the same reason the convergence pass may only append tasks: a checker that can fix can always reach a passing verdict by fixing.

decision.chose: An append-only action ledger at `.aidocs/<project>/memory/action-ledger.md`, written by the coordinator at each wave boundary and at batch close, and audited by a dedicated subagent before the next batch's INTAKE. Entries require cited evidence; the auditor may write only `status` plus an appended `resolved:` citation.
decision.rejected: BMAD's epic-end retrospective shape — one post-hoc pass mining story files at close (evidence has to be reconstructed from records written for another purpose, and attribution to a wave becomes guesswork); writing entries without the paired audit (produces a diary nobody re-reads, which is what the empty `memory/` folders already record); a free-text lessons-learned section in the run log (unfalsifiable entries cannot be closed or repeated, so they accumulate as permanent noise); letting the auditor edit an entry's observation (it can then close any entry by narrowing what it claimed).
decision.rationale: The write half and the audit half each become a no-op alone, so a workflow implementing one converges on doing neither — pairing them makes the ledger self-enforcing, because the audit gives the writing a consumer and the writing gives the audit a subject. Writing at the boundary rather than at close is where the evidence already is: the coordinator has just read the merge point, run the verify matrix and re-derived the next grouping. Auditing before INTAKE rather than after DELIVER is what makes an unaddressed entry an input to planning instead of a footnote to a finished batch. The evidence requirement is the same citation bar the review loop puts on blockers, and for the same reason: an audit against impressions can be resolved neither way, so every entry stays open forever and the ledger stops being read. The productive entry class is the coordinator catch — it means the phase that should have caught the problem is under-specified, so its remediation is a diff to a versioned file under `prompts/`, which closes the loop this pattern exists for.
